links.note: Why the civilisation has several names - this concept is the one that lists Indus, Harappan, Indus-Sarasvati and Sindhu-Sarasvati, says the chapter will use all of them, and explains that Harappan is commonest only because Harappa was excavated first in 1920-21.

A 150 to 200 word report summing up the achievements of the Indus-Sarasvati civilisation is verbatim the second of the chapter's eight closing questions, and it draws on the whole Before We Move On summary rather than on any single section.

Travel options from Harappa to Kalibangan and how long each would take is answered from this concept's land routes, rivers and sea for more distant destinations; the summary concept sets the task but carries no transport.

The four or five biggest surprises awaiting a Harappan transported to a modern Indian kitchen is verbatim the fourth of the eight closing questions, and it spans food, utensils, metal and fuel rather than one section.

Listing ornaments, gestures and objects from the chapter's pictures that still feel familiar today is the continuity argument this concept builds - the bangles covering an entire arm still worn in Gujarat and Rajasthan, and the conclusion the exercise steers towards.

The mindset reflected by the system of reservoirs at Dholavira - this concept holds the six large reservoirs cut into rock, connected by underground drains for water harvesting, and the THINK ABOUT IT about who organised and maintained them.

About 700 brick-built wells at Mohenjo-daro, regularly maintained for centuries - this concept is where people drew water from hundreds of wells made of bricks and where the need for regular cleaning implies a local authority.

Whether the Harappans had a high civic sense, compared with citizens of a large Indian city today, is the question this concept says the chapter closes with, and it only makes sense because the bathing areas and the drains running below the streets are described first.
Civilisation as the term for an advanced stage of human societies - this concept's definition, reached before the Harappans are mentioned at all.

Mesopotamia, modern Iraq and Syria, as the region where civilisation began about 6,000 years ago - this concept places the Harappans among their contemporaries and is the only one naming Mesopotamia and Egypt.

The 2600 BCE to 1900 BCE span is anchored by this concept's chronology - villages growing into towns from about 3500 BCE and towns into cities around 2600 BCE - which is the dating the chapter establishes.
The plains of Punjab and Sindh watered by the Indus and its tributaries being fertile and therefore favourable to agriculture is this concept's opening geography, word for word.

The Sarasvati flowing from the Himalayan foothills through Haryana, Punjab, parts of Rajasthan and Gujarat a few millenniums ago - this concept's sentence, distinguished from the Ganga, Yamuna and Narmada distractors.
The inhabitants are called Harappans - stated in this concept alongside the several names of the civilisation itself.
Harappa as the first city of this civilisation to be excavated, in 1920-21 - the DON'T MISS OUT box in this concept, which is also why the civilisation carries that name.
The First Urbanisation of India - this concept names that development explicitly after describing towns growing into cities around 2600 BCE. Already linked and correct.
Dholavira in Gujarat as the city known for advanced water management - this concept is the one about its six large reservoirs, the 73 metre one, and their connecting underground drains.

The Sarasvati first mentioned in the Rig Veda, an ancient collection of prayers where it is worshipped as goddess and river - this concept's sentence, which the Upanishads, Puranas and Brahmanas distractors sit against.
The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro, a small but elaborate tank of about 12 by 7 metres - this concept is the whole discussion of that structure.

The general public bath reading is ruled out because most houses in Mohenjo-daro had individual bathrooms - this concept states that elimination and leaves the royal-bath and ritual-tank readings open.
A reservoir glossed as a large natural or artificial place where water is stored appears in this concept, beside Dholavira's reservoirs.
A clay model of the plough - this concept is the one that says they made farming tools including the plough, some of which are still used by modern farmers.
Turmeric, ginger and banana remains found by scientific examination of clay pots showing a diverse diet - this concept's surprising findings, in those words.
Carnelian, a reddish semiprecious stone found mostly in Gujarat, as the most favoured bead material - this concept's own sentence, with the drilling technique beside it.

The chief purpose of the thousands of small seals being to let traders identify their goods and each other - this concept opens on exactly that inference and closes saying the seals somehow relate to trade.
The one-horned bull depicted on seals - this concept is the one describing seals that generally depict animal figures with writing signs above them, whose symbolic meaning is not yet understood.
The Lothal pot whose design tells a story like the thirsty crow fable - this concept's LET'S EXPLORE asks the reader to complete the story found on the Lothal pot. Already linked and correct.

Pairing Harappan sites with their modern states - Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira and Kalibangan are four of the five cities this concept's LET'S EXPLORE asks the class to match with modern states or regions.

The assertion that Harappans traded both internally and with distant regions is this concept's opening claim about active trade within their civilisation and with others, supported by the exported ornaments, timber, gold and cotton it lists.

The one surviving statement, that they developed a system of writing, is this concept's subject - the signs on the seals are a writing system, present but not yet readable. The item's numbered statements 1 and 2 are missing from the stem.
Urbanism defined as town-planning, the growth of cities and their management - the second of the seven characteristics this concept sets out.
Rakhigarhi in Haryana as one of the largest sites - this concept introduces it among the other major cities discovered after Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, and is where its state is stated.

Picking out absence of trade as the one thing that is not a characteristic of civilisation is decided directly against the seven characteristics this concept lists, government, urbanism, crafts, trade, writing, cultural ideas and productive agriculture.
The undeciphered script on the seals as evidence of written communication - this concept says the signs are part of a writing system that is yet to be understood. Already linked and correct.

The Dancing Girl made of bronze metal is the one correct artefact-material pair, and bronze is explained only in this concept - copper with tin added, harder than copper, used for tools, pots and pans and some figurines.
Elite glossed as the higher layers of society - rulers, officials, administrators and often priests - appears in this concept, describing who probably lived in the upper town.
Identifying destruction by an Aryan invasion as the statement that is not a known fact rests on this concept's finding that there is no trace of warfare or invasion and no army or weapons of war.

The visible statement about importing carnelian beads is judged against this concept, which has carnelian beads among the exports and copper as the likely import. Already linked and correct; the item's other numbered statements are missing from the stem.

Small steatite objects carved with bulls and unicorns plus writing-like symbols in commercial contexts are Harappan seals - this concept describes them as generally made of steatite, a few centimetres across, with animal figures and writing signs, and relating to trade.

The Priest King statuette belongs to the two pages of unearthed Harappan objects this concept covers, where the THINK ABOUT IT asks what aspects of life those objects reveal. The statuette is not named in the concept text, but this is the chapter's only section on such figurines and their significance.
The quality of construction being the same for small and big houses is this concept's own observation, stated right after individual houses of various sizes lining the streets and lanes.
Spotting Vedic Civilisation as the name that is not used is decided against this concept's list - Indus, Harappan, Indus-Sarasvati or Sindhu-Sarasvati.
Cotton allowing woven clothing - this concept says they were the first in Eurasia to grow cotton, which they used to weave into clothes. Already linked and correct.

Irrigation canals at a rural site pointing to water management - this concept opens on the Harappans giving much importance to water management and cleanliness, which is the inference the item asks for.
Ruling out wild lions among domesticated animals - this concept states they domesticated a number of animals for meat consumption and fished in rivers and the sea.

People adopting a rural lifestyle after the urban centres declined - this concept says the cities were abandoned one by one and any remaining inhabitants took up a rural lifestyle in the changed environment.
The largest reservoir at Dholavira measuring 73 metres in length - this concept gives that figure and asks the class to pace out a comparable distance.
Pulses glossed as a category of crops that includes beans, peas and lentils appears in this concept's list of what the Harappans grew.
Civilisation as the term for an advanced stage of human societies - this concept's definition; the features named in the stem are only the cue.
Naming one key characteristic that defines a civilisation is answered straight from this concept's seven - government, urbanism, crafts, trade, writing, cultural ideas and productive agriculture.
